extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary theory and criticism (critics, teachers, and writers interested in Northrop Frye's myth criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Northrop Frye's myth-criticism framework to analyze or classify literature by uncovering recurrent mythic/archetypal patterns and mapping works onto a seasonal/genre schema (romance, tragedy, irony/satire, comedy). Emphasizes a formalist, systematic approach that links texts to anthropological and psychological myth-bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypal approach / Myth Criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduced the archetypal approach called Myth Criticism (Frye's central method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret literature by identifying archetypal figures, motifs, and patterns (myths, rituals, folktales) that reappear across works and cultures. The approach combines typological biblical interpretation and Blake's conception of imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalist emphasis: criticism as scientific, objective, systematic
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye continued the formalist emphasis of New Criticism and its insistence on criticism as a scientific, objective and systematic discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus analysis on internal textual structures and regularities rather than solely on author biography or historical contingencies; aim for consistent, repeatable interpretive categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary history as a repetitive, self-contained cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary history is a repetitive and self contained cycle where basic symbolic myths (for instance the deluge, trickster) recur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating works, look for recurring mythic motifs (e.g., deluge, trickster) and patterns across periods; treat literary history as patterned rather than purely linear development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anthropological and psychological bases (rituals and folktales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Myth criticism drew upon the anthropological and psychological bases of myths; rituals and folktales to restore the spiritual content to the alienated, fragmented world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground readings in comparative material (rituals, folktales, mythic practices) and in psychological theories of myth to recover the spiritual or communal meanings in texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth-making as integral to human thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Myth criticism regarded the creation of myth (with its association with magic, imagination, dreams etc.) as integral to human thought; and myth as the collective attempt of cultures to establish a meaningful context to human existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat texts as cultural acts of meaning-making; assess how a work partakes in or creates mythic frameworks that address existential or communal needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature as emerging from a core of myth / system of recurrent patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature is viewed as emerging out of a core of myth, and as a 'system' based on 'recurrent patterns'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze texts as nodes within a larger systemic network of recurring symbolic structures rather than isolated artifacts; identify the governing patterns that structure meaning across works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link to Structuralism and Jungian collective unconscious
rubrics_metrics.description: These parameters were also reflected in other contemporary movements such as Structuralism and Jungian concept of the 'collective unconscious'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate archetypal readings within broader theoretical frameworks (structuralist patterning, Jungian archetypes) and use those theories to justify claims of recurrence and universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: The four transcendental genres as a 'central unifying myth'
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye argued that literature drew upon transcendental genres such as romance (summer), tragedy (autumn), irony/satire (winter) and comedy (spring). These four genres constitute a 'central unifying myth'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify works according to this fourfold schema; use the seasonal/genre mapping as an organizing principle to interpret tone, shape, and symbolic implications of a text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codify genres and uncover archetypal structures
rubrics_metrics.description: He further codified these genres and uncovered their basic archetypal structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each genre, identify its characteristic narrative structures, motifs, and symbolic functions; use this codification as a basis for comparative analysis and classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romance genre: quest with descent and ascent (mythopoeic equivalent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The romance is characterised by a quest theme where the hero descends into subterranean depths and danger and then rises. This descent and ascent ... constituted the 'mythopoeic' equivalent of Jung’s archetype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In works labeled 'romance', look for a quest plot with a descent-into-danger and subsequent ascent/resolution (often culminating in marriage or social reintegration); treat this movement as archetypal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal/psychological mapping of genres (comedy and satire described)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summer stands for the culmination of the year’s seasons, just as romance and marriage culminates a life. Comedy is about fantasy and wish-fulfillment and, therefore, suited to spring, while satire’s disillusioned mockery suits the coldness of winter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map psychological states and symbolic qualities to genres (e.g., comedy = fantasy/wish-fulfillment/spring; satire/irony = disillusioned mockery/winter; romance/summer = culmination/union). Use these mappings to interpret mood, symbolism, and thematic orientation of texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit claim of universality (use with awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus archetypal criticism lined supposed 'universal' psychological states with literary symbols identified as 'universal'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting universality of archetypes or symbols, be aware the claim is contested; evaluate whether purported 'universal' correspondences genuinely hold across cultures and historical contexts rather than assuming them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of basic symbolic myths to seek (deluge, trickster)
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic symbolic myths (for instance the deluge, trickster) recur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying Frye's method, specifically look for recurring mythic figures and episodes (e.g., flood/deluge narratives, trickster figures) as diagnostic signs of archetypal patterning.
